Hotel Online Reputation in Italy: Reviews, Replies and Ratings

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

Hotel online reputation in Italy is decided on three platforms at once: Google, TripAdvisor and Booking.com, each with its own rules for who can review and how scores are calculated. Hotels that manage it well combine fast, personalised replies with a steady flow of new reviews collected at check-out, and they treat the rating as a commercial asset that directly supports occupancy and room rates.

Why reviews shape hotel bookings and pricing

Review scores influence both whether a traveller books and how much they are willing to pay. On online travel agencies the score is a visible filter and a ranking factor, so a property that slips below the threshold a guest sets in the search filters simply disappears from the list, whatever its location or price.

The same logic applies to rates. Revenue managers in Rome, Florence or the Dolomites know that a hotel with a stronger and more recent rating can hold its price when competitors discount, while a weaker one is pushed to compete on price alone. Guests read the latest reviews rather than the average, which means that a run of complaints about noise or cleanliness during one busy month can affect conversion long before the overall score moves. How Google, TripAdvisor and Booking.com differ

The three platforms differ mainly in who is allowed to write a review, and that difference determines what you can realistically challenge. Booking.com accepts reviews only from guests who completed a stay booked through it, Google lets any account holder post, and TripAdvisor accepts reviews from travellers without proof of booking but runs its own fraud screening.

In practice, a fake review is easier to dispute on Google or TripAdvisor than on Booking.com, where the stay is verified. Booking reviews, however, feed the property's score on a platform that often drives the largest share of reservations for Italian independent hotels, so their tone matters even when the content cannot be removed. A response strategy that protects hotel brand reputation

Reply to every negative review and to a meaningful share of positive ones, within a few days, in the guest's language and with a specific answer to the specific complaint. Future guests read replies to judge how the hotel treats people when something goes wrong, so each response is written for them as much as for the reviewer.

What a good hotel reply contains

  • A thank-you that refers to a concrete detail of the stay, so it cannot be mistaken for a template.
  • An acknowledgement of the problem without arguing about the guest's perception.
  • A factual correction only where the review contains a clear error, such as the wrong room type or a service the hotel does not offer.
  • What has changed since: the air-conditioning replaced, the breakfast hours extended, the staff briefed.
  • An invitation to continue privately by email, never sharing booking details or personal data in public.

Hotel brand reputation suffers most from defensive replies that blame the guest or reveal information about their stay. Publicly mentioning what a guest consumed from the minibar or who accompanied them may also breach the GDPR. The tone should match the property's positioning: a luxury hotel on Lake Como and a family-run guesthouse in Puglia will not sound the same, but both should sound human. Collecting reviews at check-out without breaking the rules

The most reliable way to raise a rating sustainably is to ask every guest, at the right moment, through channels the platforms allow. The right moment is usually check-out, when the experience is fresh and reception staff can gauge satisfaction in person.

  1. Train reception to ask a simple question at departure about how the stay went, and to resolve issues on the spot before the guest leaves.
  2. Offer a short link or QR code to the Google profile on the key-card holder, the invoice folder or the farewell card.
  3. Send a post-stay email within a day or two with links to Google and TripAdvisor; Booking.com sends its own invitation, so there is no need to duplicate it.
  4. Ask everyone, not only guests who seemed happy: selecting only satisfied guests (review gating) is prohibited by Google and TripAdvisor.
  5. Never offer discounts, upgrades or gifts in exchange for a review, and never write reviews for the hotel from staff or friends.

These platform rules are reinforced by Italian consumer law. Following the EU Omnibus Directive, the Codice del Consumo treats the submission or commissioning of fake reviews as an unfair commercial practice, and the Autorità Garante della Concorrenza e del Mercato can sanction businesses that manipulate ratings.

Handling fake reviews and threats from guests

Report fake or abusive reviews through each platform's official channel, attaching evidence such as the absence of any booking under that name on the dates mentioned. Reviews written by competitors, former employees or people who never stayed at the hotel are policy violations on every major platform.

A particular problem for Italian hotels is the guest who demands a refund or a free night and threatens a negative review if refused. Keep a written record of the exchange and report it; TripAdvisor explicitly treats such threats as grounds for removal, and Google's policies cover reviews used to extort a business. Where the content becomes false and damaging statements of fact, the protection against defamation under art. 595 c.p. may also apply, although a legal route is proportionate only in serious cases.

A hotel cannot control what guests write, but it can control how quickly it answers, how consistently it asks for reviews and how carefully it documents abuse.

Monitoring hotel web reputation beyond reviews

Hotel web reputation also includes what appears when someone searches the property name: news, forum threads, social media videos and, increasingly, AI-generated summaries of reviews. A viral video about bedbugs or a local news story about a dispute with staff can outweigh hundreds of positive ratings.

Set up a weekly check of branded searches on Google in Italian and in the main source markets' languages, the review dashboards of each platform and mentions on Instagram and TikTok. Assign one person to own replies and escalation, so that serious cases reach the general manager on the same day.
